source.notes: Found via the official page https://cisce.org/specimen-question-papers-isc-class-xii-2027/. The PDF contains the Chemistry Paper 1 (Theory) Specimen Question Paper (10 printed pages, PDF pages 1-10) immediately followed in the same file by its own 'ANSWER KEY' (11 printed pages of its own numbering, PDF pages 11-21); answerSourceUrl is therefore the same URL as sourceUrl and answerSourceFile is null, as instructed. Maximum Marks 70, Time Allotted Three Hours (durationMinutes=180) plus an additional fifteen minutes reading time (noted here, not added to durationMinutes). Printed instructions: 21 questions across four sections - Section A (Question 1, 14 subparts, 1 mark each, 14 marks), Section B (Questions 2-11, ten questions, 2 marks each, 20 marks), Section C (Questions 12-18, seven questions, 3 marks each, 21 marks), Section D (Questions 19-21, three questions, 5 marks each, 15 marks); 14+20+21+15=70 matches maxMarks. Internal choice ('Internal choices have been provided in two questions each in Sections B, C and D'): Questions 4 and 9 (Section B), 14 and 17 (Section C), 19 and 21 (Section D) each print an 'OR' splitting the question into two alternatives. Each alternative is entered as its own question sharing choiceGroup = the question number; the 'part' field is the roman-numeral label that begins that alternative as printed in the PDF. In three cases the OR divides unevenly across the printed sub-numbering: Question 14's first alternative is '(i)+(ii)' together (part recorded as '(i)') and its second alternative is '(iii)' alone; Question 19's first alternative is '(i)' alone and its second alternative is '(ii)+(iii)' together (part recorded as '(ii)', with (iii) embedded in the same entry's text since the PDF prints (iii) directly after (ii) with no further 'OR', i.e. (iii) belongs to whichever answer starts on the (ii) side of that specific OR). Because both alternatives of every OR pair are entered at their full printed mark value, the pack's marks sum to 90 (14 Section A + 24 Section B + 27 Section C + 25 Section D), not 70: a candidate only answers one side of each of the six OR pairs (Question 4: 2, 9: 2, 14: 3, 17: 3, 19: 5, 21: 5 = 20 extra marks) to reach the printed maximum of 70. This is expected and not an error, matching the approach used in the ICSE Class 10 specimen packs in this project. Question 1(C) is a shared reading passage (about alcohols/phenols, bracketed '[3x1]') with three separately 1-mark-each sub-questions (i)-(iii); each is entered as its own SHORT_ANSWER entry with the full passage reproduced in its text (since it is needed context), rather than merged into one case-based entry, because the paper itself marks them as three separate 1-mark items. Question 1(A)'s four fill-in-the-blank items share one printed word bank ('methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol, paired, one, Cannizzaro, d-d, salicylaldehyde, Perkin's, unpaired, f-f, salicylic acid, Kolbe's, two, 193000, 96500, Reimer-Tiemann'); this is noted per item rather than repeated in the text. Where a combined bracket (e.g. '[2]' or '[3]') covers several top-level, independently-answerable sub-items with no further per-item bracket, and the number of items divides the total evenly, the sub-items were split with marksSource SECTION_INSTRUCTIONS and an assumed even split (Questions 6, 7, 15, 16, 18). Where such a split is NOT even or the sub-items do not stand alone independently, the sub-items were kept together as one entry instead (Question 13's (i) vs (ii)(a)-(c); Question 20's (i)/(ii)/(iii), which carries the whole printed '[5]' with no OR so no split was needed or invented). Chemistry-specific extraction notes: chemical formula subscripts and ionic charges came out flat throughout the text layer (e.g. H2SO4, CoCl3.6NH3, Mg2+, OH-1) and are kept as printed, flagged per question. Purely mathematical notation (scientific-notation exponents such as '10-4', rate-law fractional exponents such as '[A]1/2[B]3/2', degree symbols flattened to plain numerals) was rebuilt inline only where the layout makes it unambiguous, per question, with confidence set to MEDIUM and an extractionIssue noting the rebuild. Structural formulas and reaction schemes drawn as diagrams (the d-orbital splitting diagram in Question 4(ii); the coupling/Balz-Schiemann reaction schemes in Question 9(i); the reagent-over-arrow reaction chains in Question 19(ii); the cis/trans platinum structures and octahedral cobalt complex structure in the Question 20 answer key) were never redrawn or invented; hasFigure is set true on the question where a diagram is needed to answer it, and where only the OFFICIAL ANSWER contains a lost structure/diagram this is flagged via extractionIssues on that entry per the 'Official answer partly missing in extraction' rule instead. Branched structural formulas in official answers that were spread across lines by the PDF layout (e.g. Question 3's compounds [A] and [C]) are reproduced using the same linear fragment the text layer extracted, annotated '(with a CH3 branch, as printed)' rather than redrawn, and flagged for verification against the PDF; nothing was written or drawn from scratch. Question 1(B)(v)'s four MCQ options each end in a blank after the reaction arrow ('C2H5NC -> LiAlH4 _________') in the extracted text; this is flagged as a probable loss of the reaction-product structure from each option (hasFigure true), though the option text needed to identify the correct answer (reactant + reagent) remained legible. Question 17(ii)'s official answer restates 'Λmo (CH3COO)2Mg = 126.9' in its own printed 'Given' line, which duplicates the NaI value and conflicts with 187.8 (the value the same answer actually uses in its calculation, matching the question's own printed data); this is reproduced verbatim as printed in the marking scheme, not corrected, and flagged. Chapter mapping: the valid chapter list for icse/12/chemistry (from `node scripts/check-sources.mjs --chapters icse 12 chemistry`) has no chapter for radioactivity/nuclear chemistry; Question 5 (a half-life/radioactive-decay numerical) was mapped to the nearest genuinely related chapter, chemical-kinetics, since the half-life and first-order-decay mathematics used to solve it is taught there; this is flagged as an approximate mapping rather than left null, since it is not a wild guess. No question in this pack was left with chapter: null.

questions.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

The hydroxy derivatives of aliphatic hydrocarbons are called alcohols. Ethanol is perhaps the most important aliphatic alcohol. During COVID-19 pandemic alcohol-based sanitizers became an essential protective tool worldwide, reducing the spread of the virus. Nowadays, it is also used as a substitute for petrol in internal combustion engines.

The boiling points of alcohols are considerably higher than those of the corresponding ethers due to the presence of intermolecular hydrogen bonding in alcohols and it increases with increase in molecular mass. For isomeric alcohols the boiling point follows the order: Primary (1°) alcohol > Secondary (2°) alcohol > Tertiary (3°) alcohol, which is evident from the following data:

Compound: Propan-1-ol, Butan-1-ol, Butan-2-ol, 2-methyl-propan-2-ol
Boiling point: 370K, 391K, 371K, 356K

Aliphatic alcohols behave as weak acids and ionize to a small extent. Their acidic strength is even less than that of both water and phenol. Phenols are hydroxy derivatives of arenes and have varied application in manufacturing of dyes, plastics, drugs, explosives, etc. At different concentrations, phenols are used both as a disinfectant and an antiseptic.

The boiling point of 2-methyl-propan-2-ol is much lower than that of butan-1-ol, although both have the same molecular formula. Give a reason to explain such observation.
extractionIssues: Passage shared with the other parts of Question 1(C); reproduced in full in each entry's text since it is necessary context.
Table (boiling points of four alcohols) reconstructed from the printed layout; check against the PDF.
Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout (degree symbols: 1°, 2°, 3° for primary/secondary/tertiary); check against the PDF.

officialAnswer.text: The boiling point of 2-methyl propan-2-ol is much lower than that of butan-1-ol. This is due to the fact that with branching the surface area decreases. Consequently, boiling point also decreases.

The boiling points of alcohols are considerably higher than those of the corresponding ethers due to the presence of intermolecular hydrogen bonding in alcohols and it increases with increase in molecular mass. For isomeric alcohols the boiling point follows the order: Primary (1°) alcohol > Secondary (2°) alcohol > Tertiary (3°) alcohol, which is evident from the following data:

Compound: Propan-1-ol, Butan-1-ol, Butan-2-ol, 2-methyl-propan-2-ol
Boiling point: 370K, 391K, 371K, 356K

Aliphatic alcohols behave as weak acids and ionize to a small extent. Their acidic strength is even less than that of both water and phenol. Phenols are hydroxy derivatives of arenes and have varied application in manufacturing of dyes, plastics, drugs, explosives, etc. At different concentrations, phenols are used both as a disinfectant and an antiseptic.

Although alcohols are weaker acids than water, phenol is more acidic than alcohols. Justify.
extractionIssues: Passage shared with the other parts of Question 1(C); reproduced in full in each entry's text since it is necessary context.
Table (boiling points of four alcohols) reconstructed from the printed layout; check against the PDF.
Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout (degree symbols: 1°, 2°, 3° for primary/secondary/tertiary); check against the PDF.

officialAnswer.text: The greater acidic character of phenol as compared to alcohols can be explained on the basis of resonance. The oxygen attracts the electron pair of O-H bond strongly towards itself, weakens the O-H bond and therefore facilitates the release of H+ more easily.

questions.text:
The standard reduction electrode potential (E°) of some metals is given below:

Metal: Ag+/Ag, Mg2+/Mg, Li+/Li, Cu2+/Cu, Fe2+/Fe
E°: +0·80V, -2·37V, -3·05V, +0·34V, -0·44V

Arrange these metals in the increasing order of their reducing power. Justify the order.
extractionIssues: Table (standard reduction potentials of five metals) reconstructed from the printed layout; check against the PDF.
Superscripts/subscripts flattened: Ag+/Ag, Mg2+/Mg, Li+/Li, Cu2+/Cu, Fe2+/Fe.

officialAnswer.text:
Increasing order of reducing power of metals is Ag < Cu < Fe < Mg < Li.
Reducing power = 1 / Reduction potential, i.e., as the reduction potential (value of metal) decreases, reducing power of metal increases.

questions.text:
An alkene [A] with molecular formula, C5H10 on ozonolysis and subsequent hydrolysis gives a mixture of two compounds, [B] and [C]. Compound [B] gives positive Fehling's test and also reacts with iodine and NaOH solution. Compound [C] does not give Fehling's test but forms iodoform.

Identify compounds [A], [B] and [C]. Write the iodoform reaction either with compound [B] or [C].
extractionIssues: Subscript flattened: C5H10.

Official answer's structural formulas for compounds [A] and [C] (branched, drawn across multiple lines with a CH3 substituent) are reproduced using the same linear fragment the text layer extracted, annotated 'with a CH3 branch, as printed' rather than redrawn; verify against the PDF.
Subscripts flattened in the official answer: CH3CHO, NaOH, CHI3, NaI, HCOONa, H2O, CH3COONa.
The marking scheme's own answer for [B] reads 'CH3CHO or acetaldehyde or ethanol' verbatim (ethanol appears to be a typo for ethanal in the marking scheme); reproduced as printed, not corrected.

officialAnswer.text:
[A] CH3–CH=C–CH3 (with a CH3 branch, as printed) or 2-methyl but-2-ene
[B] CH3CHO or acetaldehyde or ethanol
[C] CH3–C=O (with a CH3 branch, as printed) or propanone or acetone

Iodoform reaction with compound [B]:
CH3CHO + 3I2 + 4NaOH →(Δ) CHI3 + 3NaI + HCOONa + 3H2O

Or, iodoform reaction with compound [C]:
CH3–C=O (with a CH3 branch) + 3I2 + 4NaOH →(Δ) CHI3 + 3NaI + CH3COONa + 3H2O

questions.text:
Rohan, a patient of thyroid disorder, was given certain amount of radioactive Iodine-131 as a part of his treatment.

What amount of Iodine-131 will be left in Rohan's body after 48 days, if it is known that the half-life period of radioactive iodine-131 is 12 days? Assume that no amount of the isotope was eliminated through biological processes.
extractionIssues: Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout (fractions/powers in the half-life calculation); check against the PDF.

Chapter mapping note: this radioactivity/half-life problem has no dedicated chapter in the valid ICSE Class 12 Chemistry chapter list; mapped to the nearest related chapter (chemical-kinetics) since the half-life/first-order-decay mathematics is taught there.

officialAnswer.text:
Given: t1/2 = 12 days, t = 48 days.
Number of half lives = Total time / Half life period = 48/12 = 4
Amount left after 4 half lives: A = Ao × (1/2)^4 = Ao × 1/16
i.e., 1/16 of the initial amount.

questions.text:
Substantiate the following statement with a reason.
Cobalt is attracted in a magnetic field whereas Zinc is not.
(Atomic number of Co = 27 and Zn =30)
extractionIssues: Split from the shared instruction 'Substantiate the following statements with reasons.' and combined mark [2] printed once for (i)-(ii); assumed 1 mark each (even split).
Subscripts flattened: d7, d10.

officialAnswer.text:
Cobalt has d7 electrons in the outer shell and therefore, has three unpaired electrons. Therefore, it will be attracted in a magnetic field.
Zinc has completely filled d10 configuration and therefore, will not be attracted by the magnetic field.

Two students Rehan and Ananya were given the same compound, alkyl halide (C2H5Cl) by their chemistry teacher and asked to perform different reactions.

• Rehan was instructed to use alcoholic KCN as a reagent and Ananya was instructed to use alcoholic AgCN.
• Rehan observed a compound was formed that could be converted to a carboxylic acid on hydrolysis but Ananya could not obtain the same acid.
• The teacher explained that the difference was due to the bonding behaviour of cyanide ions in the reagents.

Write the chemical equations of the reactions and the IUPAC names of the compounds formed by Rehan and Ananya.
extractionIssues: Subscripts flattened: C2H5Cl, KCN, AgCN.

Rehan's Reaction: C2H5Cl + KCN →(alc) C2H5CN + KCl (Propane nitrile)

(i) For a given first order reaction, it takes 5 minutes for the initial concentration of 0·6 moles litre-1 to become 0·2 moles litre-1. Calculate the rate constant for this reaction.

(ii) Find the overall order of the reactions which have the following rate law expression:
(a) Rate = k[A]^(1/2)[B]^(3/2)
(b) Rate = k[A]^(3/2)[B]^-1
(c) Rate = k[A]^1[B]^2

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Given: t = 5 minutes, a = 0.6 moles litre-1, (a−x) = 0.2 moles litre-1
K = (2.303/t) log10 [a/(a−x)] = (2.303/5) log10 (0.6/0.2) = (2.303/5) log 3 = (2.303 × 0.477)/5
K = 0.2197 min-1

(ii)(a) Rate = k[A]^(1/2)[B]^(3/2): overall order = 1/2 + 3/2 = 2
(b) Rate = k[A]^(3/2)[B]^-1: overall order = 3/2 − 1 = 1/2

(c) The molecular weight of potassium chloride and sucrose is determined by the depression of freezing point method. Compared to their theoretical molecular weight, what will be their observed molecular weights when determined by the above method? Justify your answer.

(a) Given: π = 3.05×10^-3 atm, T = 298K, V = 300/1000 = 0.3 L, w = 1.85 g
π = CRT = (w×R×T)/(m×V)
m = (1.85 × 0.0821 × 298) / (3.05×10^-3 × 0.3)

(b) Given: kf = 5.12 K kg mol-1, ΔTf = 0.85K, m = 94 g mol-1, w = 2.5 g, W = 120 g, n = 2

i = M(normal)/M(observed) = 94/125.49 = 0.749
α (degree of association) = (1−i)/(1−1/n) = (1−0.749)/(1−1/2) = 0.251/0.5 = 0.502 or 50.2%

(c) The observed molecular mass of potassium chloride will be half of its theoretical molecular mass. The depression in freezing point is a colligative property which depends upon the number of solute particles present in solution. KCl is a strong electrolyte; it furnishes two ions, KCl → K+ + Cl-.
The observed molecular mass of sucrose as determined by the depression in freezing point method will be the same as the theoretical molecular mass.

questions.text:
(a) Arrange the following aqueous solutions in increasing order of osmotic pressure. Give reasons in support of your answer.
(1) 6·0g per litre of urea solution (molecular weight of urea = 60g mol-1)
(2) 72·0g per litre of glucose solution (molecular weight of glucose = 180g mol-1)
(3) 5·85g per litre of sodium chloride solution (molecular weight of sodium chloride = 58·5g mol-1)

(b) Calculate the mole fraction (x) of ethanol and water if 92g of ethanol is dissolved in 540g of water.
(Atomic mass of C = 12, O = 16 and H = 1)

(c) What type of azeotropic mixture will be formed by a solution of chloroform and acetone? Justify your answer based on strength of intermolecular interactions that develops in the solution.
extractionIssues: This is the other of two OR alternatives for Question 21 (choiceGroup 21); the candidate answers only (i) or (ii).
Marks not itemised across (a)-(c) (only the combined [5] for the whole alternative is printed); kept together as one entry.
Sub-parts carry different printed cognitive tags: (a) Analyse, (b) Apply, (c) Evaluate; no single cognitiveLevel recorded.
Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout (fractions in the mole-fraction and mole calculations); check against the PDF.

officialAnswer.text:
(a) Osmotic pressure ∝ number of solute particles.
(1) Moles of urea = 6/60 = 0.1 mol → 0.1 × 6.023×10^23 = 6.023×10^22 particles
(2) Moles of glucose = 72/180 = 0.4 mol → 0.4 × 6.023×10^23 = 24.092×10^22 particles
(3) Moles of NaCl = 5.85/58.5 = 0.1 mol; NaCl → Na+ + Cl-, so 0.1 mol NaCl → 2 × 6.023×10^23 × 0.1 = 12.046×10^22 particles
Therefore, increasing order of osmotic pressure is: Urea < NaCl < glucose

(b) Given: wt. of C2H5OH = 92 g, wt. of H2O = 540 g, mol. wt. of C2H5OH = 46 g mol-1, mol. wt. of H2O = 18 g mol-1
No. of moles of C2H5OH (n) = 92/46 = 2 moles
No. of moles of H2O (N) = 540/18 = 30 moles
Mole fraction of C2H5OH = n/(n+N) = 2/32 = 0.0625
Mole fraction of water = N/(n+N) = 30/32 = 0.9375

(c) The mixture of chloroform and acetone is an example of maximum boiling azeotrope. It shows negative deviation from Raoult's Law because of the increase in intermolecular forces of attraction between chloroform and acetone, since they form hydrogen bonds between them.
